questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a before and after comparison needs a counterfactual
questions.stem: A pond survey records more dragonfly larvae after a bank work, and the biologist must explain what the survey has and has not shown.

options.text: More larvae after the work shows the work helped, provided the pond would have been similar anyway
More larvae after the work proves the work helped, because the pond could not change on its own
options.misconception: ignores the possibility of natural year to year change

options.text: More larvae after the work proves the work helped, because the pond has no other source of larvae
options.misconception: assumes there is only one possible source of the animals

options.text: More larvae after the work proves nothing at all, so the survey record should be discarded
options.misconception: overstates the value of the comparison

questions.explanation: A before and after count shows an effect only if the pond would otherwise have been similar, which is what the counterfactual supplies. Weather alone can produce the same rise.
questions.hint: Ask what would have happened without the work.

questions.stem: A grassland plot has a runoff coefficient of 0.15 and an equally sized neighbouring plot now under dense scrub has 0.40, and the biologist must compute the weighted runoff coefficient for the site.
questions.explanation: Equal areas give an average of the two coefficients, so 0.15 plus 0.40 divided by two is 0.275. The increase comes entirely from the scrub plot, where interception and infiltration are lower.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a sampling scheme that separates concentration from mass load
questions.stem: A biologist must report both concentration and mass load of suspended sediment in a stream, and the sampling design must support both.

answer.exemplar: Sample the cross section at a set of points spanning the channel on a fixed interval through the discharge cycle, measuring velocity and depth at each point so that flow can be integrated across the section. Pair every flow sample with a sediment concentration sample and multiply the two to obtain a load, then report the load over the whole sampling day as well as the mean concentration. Sampling concentration alone will mislead whenever discharge varies, so the flow record must accompany every laboratory result.

questions.explanation: Concentration without flow cannot give a load, so the design must measure flow across the section and pair it with concentration. Sampling across the discharge cycle prevents one lucky moment.
questions.hint: You cannot have a load without a flow.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why sequential reductions must be multiplied rather than added
questions.stem: Two treatment stages each remove a proportion of what reaches them, and the biologist must explain how the combined removal is worked out.

answer.exemplar: Each stage acts on the material that survives the previous one, so the fraction passing through the pair is the product of the two survival fractions rather than the sum of them. If the first removes 40 per cent and the second removes 50 per cent of what arrives, then 0.6 times 0.5, which is 0.3, remains and the combined removal is 70 per cent. Adding the percentages would give 90 per cent, which cannot be right because nothing can be removed twice.

questions.explanation: Each stage removes a share of what is left, so the survival fractions multiply and removals must not simply be added. Treating them as independent shares of the original load overstates the pair.
questions.hint: Work with the fraction that survives each stage.

questions.explanation: A drawdown of 1.4 metres exceeds the stated threshold of 0.8 metres, so the conclusion follows from the figures given. The judgement still depends on the threshold in force and the baseline used.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Runoff coefficient change with land cover
questions.learningObjective: Design a test of how land cover changes a runoff coefficient
questions.stem: A biologist must show how replacing grassland with scrub changes the runoff coefficient of a field, and the design must be defensible.

answer.exemplar: Install replicated plots of the two cover types on comparable soil, and measure the volume of runoff generated by a fixed applied depth of water under controlled conditions over several wetting cycles. Derive a coefficient from the ratio of runoff to applied water for each plot, then compare the distributions with a rank test rather than comparing single values. Replicate plots on different soils and repeat across seasons, since a single wetting after installation gives a wet or dry soil state that will not represent the long-term condition.

questions.explanation: Replicated plots under controlled application give a coefficient per plot that can be compared statistically, and repeating across soils and seasons avoids a result from one transient wetting.
questions.hint: Replicate the plots and repeat the wetting.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why concentration and mass load can move in opposite directions
questions.stem: A stream shows a rising suspended sediment concentration and a falling daily sediment load, and the biologist must explain the discrepancy.

answer.exemplar: Concentration is mass per unit volume of water while load is mass per unit time, and the flow between them changes the picture completely. If the discharge falls sharply while the concentration rises less steeply, the mass arriving each day can fall even though each litre is dirtier. Any statement about sediment risk has to name which of the two quantities it refers to, because conclusions drawn from concentration alone can be the opposite of those drawn from the load.

questions.explanation: Concentration is mass per volume and load is mass per time, so a falling discharge can cut the daily load while the concentration rises. Statements must name which quantity they describe.
questions.hint: One is per litre, the other is per day.

questions.explanation: Removing half and then half of the remainder leaves a quarter, so the combined removal is three quarters. Each stage acts on what the previous stage passed on.
questions.hint: Apply the second stage to what the first stage leaves.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a survey that detects effort shifting after a ban
questions.stem: A closure has been introduced on one fishing method, and the biologist must design a survey that can tell whether the effort has simply moved.

answer.exemplar: Record the same effort indicators before and after the closure, including vessel activity by method, gear deployment, landings at the market and any activity in nearby waters, using the same questions and reporting limits before and after. Pair the fishery data with independent counts of activity and with the number of observed violations, so that a fall in reported landings can be separated from a fall in real activity. The comparison must cover a full season, since effort shifts within weeks and settles quickly.

questions.explanation: Effort indicators collected the same way before and after the closure show whether activity moved elsewhere, while market landings reveal whether any fall in reported catch is real.
questions.hint: Collect the same effort data before and after.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Runoff coefficient change with land cover
questions.learningObjective: Explain how vegetation cover alters a runoff coefficient
questions.stem: A field's runoff coefficient rises from 0.10 to 0.25 after grassland is replaced by bare cultivated soil, and the biologist must explain the change.

answer.exemplar: Bare cultivated soil has little roughness to slow the moving water and no litter or root mat to hold it, so a much larger share of the rain reaches the surface flow rather than soaking into the ground. Because the coefficient is the ratio of that runoff to the rainfall applied, the value rises with the increase in fast surface flow. Intercepted water on vegetation, slower delivery and greater infiltration all push the coefficient down, which is why rough perennial cover keeps it low.

questions.explanation: Bare soil loses the litter, roughness and root mat that slow water and let it infiltrate, so more rainfall becomes surface runoff. Vegetation acts the other way on each route.
questions.hint: Think about what cover does to infiltration.

questions.learningObjective: Design a study that separates a lagged response from a coincidental one
questions.stem: A species rises in the year a regulation starts, and the biologist must design a study that can separate a lagged effect from a coincidental one.

answer.exemplar: Combine the regulated area with a comparable unregulated area, and sample both over several years so that any lagged response in the regulated area can be compared with the trend in the untreated one. Keep the sampling method and season identical across areas and years, and add a before period of at least two years so the pre-existing trends are known. Where regulations apply in patches, a stepped design with untreated patches inside the treated area gives an additional comparison.

questions.explanation: A comparison area sampled over the same years gives the trend that would have happened anyway, so divergence can be attributed to the regulation. Before and after data make it meaningful.
questions.hint: Include an untreated area sampled the same way.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a ban on one activity can raise pressure elsewhere
questions.stem: A ban closes a popular public footpath on a headland, and the biologist must explain the effect that follows for the wildlife there.

answer.exemplar: Closing the headland footpath removes the most regular walking pressure from the tightest dune and saltmarsh habitat, but it also removes the reason visitors came, so displaced walkers seek the next nearest vantage point, often a path along the sheltered bay where ground nesting birds are concentrated. The measured effects on the closed site and the substitution site therefore have to be considered together, and a monitoring scheme that watches only the protected area will misread the result.

questions.explanation: Removing one source of pressure often moves it to the next best place, so gains at the closed path can be offset by losses nearby. Monitoring must include the substitution sites.
questions.hint: Ask where people will go instead.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish concentration from mass load in a sediment record
questions.stem: A biologist must choose between reporting a concentration value and a mass load for a stream, and the choice must be appropriate to the question.

options.text: Report the concentration, because it measures the pollution risk to organisms in the water
options.misconception: assumes concentration alone describes the risk to organisms

options.text: Report the mass load, because it measures how much material reaches the watercourse in a day
Report the concentration, because it is the quantity that the permits are written against
options.misconception: assumes permits are set on concentration alone

options.text: Report the mass load, because it can be measured without recording the flow
options.misconception: believes a load can be measured without flow

questions.explanation: Concentration describes how dirty a volume of water is, while the load describes how much material arrives in a period, which drives downstream deposition. A load cannot be calculated without flow.
questions.hint: Which one needs the flow to exist at all?

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Read a staged treatment record and check the compounded result
questions.stem: A reed bed removes 60 per cent of the phosphorus in the water entering it and a following wetland removes 70 per cent of what reaches it, and the biologist must check the claim made for the pair.

options.text: The pair removes 95 per cent, because the two removals can be added together
options.misconception: adds percentages taken from different baselines

options.text: The pair removes 30 per cent, because the second stage undoes some of the first
options.misconception: assumes a second stage returns material to the flow

options.text: The pair removes 82 per cent, because 0.4 times 0.3 leaves 0.12 of the phosphorus
The pair removes 88 per cent, because the first stage works better when the second follows it
options.misconception: invents an interaction between the two stages

questions.explanation: The reed bed leaves 40 per cent and the wetland removes 70 per cent of that, so 0.4 times 0.3 leaves 0.12 and 82 per cent is removed. Adding the percentages would give an impossible 95 per cent.
questions.hint: Multiply the fractions that survive each stage.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Read a threshold diagram for a groundwater scheme
questions.stem: A diagram shows the drawdown threshold, the observed well level and the site features, and the biologist must read the position.

options.text: The well stays within the threshold, because its level is lower than the threshold line
options.misconception: reads the axis of a depth against a drawdown value

options.text: The well stays within the threshold, because the line is drawn above the observed level
options.misconception: reads a diagram without checking the axis direction

options.text: The well breaches the threshold, because the observed level is below the line on the diagram
options.misconception: confuses a depth with the permitted drawdown

options.text: The well breaches the threshold, because the drawdown from the start level exceeds the permitted figure

questions.explanation: The threshold is a permitted drawdown from the start level, so the test compares how far the level has fallen, not where a line sits on the axis. Exceeding the figure is a breach.
questions.hint: Work out the fall from the starting level.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Calculate how many paired comparisons remain after points are lost
questions.stem: A pond survey uses fifteen paired sampling points, but four of the after points cannot be matched because a dredging campaign moved the markers, and the biologist must calculate how many paired comparisons remain.
questions.explanation: Four of the fifteen paired points lose their partner after the dredging, so eleven matched comparisons remain. Unpaired points must be dropped rather than counted as no change.
questions.hint: Subtract the unmatched points from the total.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a control scheme for a large scale field intervention
questions.stem: A wide area is to be grazed differently, and the biologist must design a control arrangement that will hold up to scrutiny.

answer.exemplar: Select control sites by matching soil type, slope, aspect and past management from a longer baseline record, and spread the controls across the landscape rather than placing them all on the easiest land. Pair each treated unit with a control unit drawn at random from the matched pool, and keep the treatment and control units far enough apart that the grazers do not spill across the boundary. Record any management that happens outside the planned scheme, since an unrecorded intervention on a control site ends its usefulness.

questions.explanation: Controls inform only if they resemble the treated units in everything but the treatment, so selection must use soil and history. Separation and outside management records protect the comparison.
questions.hint: Match controls on soil, slope and history.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a response before the intervention cannot be attributed to it
questions.stem: A species population rises in the two years before a habitat work begins, and the biologist must explain what that does to the attribution.

answer.exemplar: A rise that begins before the intervention cannot be caused by it, so any claim that the work produced the increase is contradicted by the timing of the record. The pre-intervention trend also supplies the baseline against which the later response should be judged: if the population was already climbing at a given rate, the work should be credited only with the amount above that projected trend. Extrapolating the pre-intervention rate forward, rather than assuming a flat baseline, is the usual error in this situation.

questions.explanation: A rise starting before the work cannot be caused by it, and the pre-intervention trend gives the baseline for what followed. Crediting the work with the whole rise ignores that trend.
questions.hint: Check whether the change came first.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Assess a banning notice for evidence of effort displacement

stimulus.body: The notice prohibits the damaging activity within the boundary of the designated site. It records no monitoring of the activity on adjacent land, and the activity requires equipment that can be moved a short distance without additional cost or permission.

questions.stem: A banning notice is issued for a damaging activity on one stretch of coast, and the biologist must advise the authority on its likely effect.

options.text: The notice may not reduce the activity, because it can simply continue just outside the boundary
The notice will certainly reduce the activity, because the boundary is drawn around the worst damage
options.misconception: assumes the boundary choice guarantees compliance

options.text: The notice is irrelevant, because damaging activity always damages places outside the boundary
options.misconception: overgeneralises about activity beyond the site

options.text: The notice is effective only if the damaging activity is also banned in every other country
options.misconception: invents an international requirement

questions.explanation: A boundary restriction leaves the activity available just outside it, and low relocation costs make displacement likelier than abandonment. Monitoring nearby shows whether the burden moved.
questions.hint: What is the easiest response to a boundary rule?

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Runoff coefficient change with land cover
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a land cover change alters a runoff coefficient
questions.stem: A field's measured runoff coefficient falls after it is planted with a cover crop, and the biologist must explain the change.

options.text: The coefficient falls because cover crops reduce the amount of rainfall that reaches the ground
options.misconception: assumes a cover crop intercepts rainfall before it lands

options.text: The coefficient falls because the cover slows water and lets more of it infiltrate the soil
The coefficient falls because cover crops evaporate the rainfall before the measurement starts
options.misconception: invents an evaporation term for the measurement period

options.text: The coefficient falls because the measurement was taken while the soil was frozen
options.misconception: invents a soil condition not recorded

questions.explanation: A cover crop adds roughness and a root mat that slow water and open pores for infiltration, so less rainfall leaves as surface runoff. The coefficient is runoff over rainfall.
questions.hint: The ratio falls when the runoff part falls.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a record where concentration and load move differently
questions.stem: At a small stream the mean sediment concentration doubles between two years while mean discharge halves, and the biologist must work out the effect on the load.

options.text: The daily load has doubled, because concentration doubled
options.misconception: ignores the halving of discharge

options.text: The daily load has halved, because discharge halved
options.misconception: ignores the doubling of concentration

options.text: The daily load is unchanged, because the two changes cancel each other
The daily load has fallen by a quarter, because the changes do not cancel exactly
options.misconception: invents a third factor in the calculation

questions.explanation: Load is concentration times discharge, so doubling the concentration while halving the discharge leaves the product unchanged. Reading either number alone gives the wrong direction of change.
questions.hint: Multiply the two quantities together.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Read a treatment train diagram and check the compounded result
questions.stem: A diagram shows two treatment stages in series, each removing a stated share of what reaches it, and the biologist must read the combined effect.

options.text: The train removes 75 per cent, because the two stages each remove 50 per cent of the original load
options.misconception: treats each stage as acting on the original load

options.text: The train removes 50 per cent, because only the first stage does any work
options.misconception: ignores the second stage entirely

options.text: The train removes 90 per cent, because the two shares can be added together
options.misconception: adds shares taken from different baselines

options.text: The train removes 75 per cent, because the second stage acts on the half that survives

questions.explanation: If the first stage removes half, the second takes half of the remaining half, leaving a quarter behind and removing 75 per cent overall. Adding the shares claims an impossible removal.
questions.hint: Follow the material through both stages.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose a drawdown assessment that measures from the wrong baseline
questions.stem: A report judges a well against a drawdown threshold by comparing the observed level with the threshold figure directly, and the biologist must find the flaw.

options.text: The flaw is that the threshold is a fall in level, not a level itself, so the two cannot be compared
The flaw is that the report should have used a pressure transducer rather than a dipper
options.misconception: focuses on the instrument instead of the comparison

options.text: The flaw is that the well should have been measured at least twice each week throughout
options.misconception: focuses on visit frequency rather than the comparison

options.text: The flaw is that a threshold can only be applied to wells within a designated area
options.misconception: invents a geographic restriction on thresholds

questions.explanation: A drawdown threshold is a permitted fall from a baseline, so it must be compared with the difference between observed and starting levels. Setting a level against a fall figure mixes quantities.
questions.hint: A drawdown is a difference, not a level.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a study that supplies the missing counterfactual for a grazing change
questions.stem: A field has been taken out of grazing and its ground cover has changed, and the biologist must design a study that shows what the change actually caused.

answer.exemplar: Select a comparable ungrazed field with the same soil, slope and aspect that has been ungrazed throughout, and record the vegetation, invertebrates and bare ground on both each spring and late summer for at least three years. Pair the two fields on each date and analyse the difference in change, not the raw difference in state, so that a wet year that affects both fields cancels out. Where the history of the ungrazed field is uncertain, use several candidate controls and report how sensitive the result is to that choice.

questions.explanation: A long-matched ungrazed field supplies the missing comparison, and pairing by date removes the shared effect of weather. Comparing changes rather than states protects the result.
questions.hint: Find a comparable field and pair the dates.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a control site must be chosen before the intervention
questions.stem: A conservation team chooses its control site after the intervention has begun, and the biologist must explain the risk this creates.

answer.exemplar: A control chosen after the works may have been selected precisely because it looks different from the treated site, which is the opposite of what a control is for. Matching on soil, slope, aspect and management has to be done on records that predate the intervention, otherwise the selection is influenced by the outcome and any comparison is circular. Choosing controls in advance, and stating the matching criteria and how similar the sites proved to be, keeps the comparison honest and lets a reader judge how much confidence to place in it.

questions.explanation: Choosing a control after the works risks selecting it because it differs from the treated site, defeating the purpose. Matching must use pre-intervention records, and the achieved similarity reported.
questions.hint: A control picked afterwards is chosen for the wrong reason.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Review an attribution claim for the strength of its timing evidence

stimulus.body: The extract states that the colony increased from 32 to 95 breeding pairs in the ten years following the reduction in grazing, that grazing was reduced over a single winter, and that the site has also been affected by a rising sea level over the same period.

questions.stem: A review claims that a colony benefits from a grazing reduction because the colony grew in the following decade, and the biologist must judge the claim.

options.text: The claim is proved, because a ten year increase cannot plausibly be caused by a single winter of management
options.misconception: assumes long changes cannot follow management

options.text: The claim is weakened by a second change over the same period and the absence of a comparison site
The claim is wrong, because breeding pairs cannot be counted reliably over ten years
options.misconception: invents a counting limitation

options.text: The claim is wrong, because grazing reduction always reduces breeding pairs in saltmarsh habitats
options.misconception: states a false general rule about grazing and birds

questions.explanation: A rising sea level over the same decade offers an alternative explanation, and without a comparison site the increase cannot be pinned on the grazing reduction. Timing fits but does not establish it.
questions.hint: Look for other changes over the same period.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the mechanism by which a ban transfers a burden
questions.stem: A ban on a fishing method is introduced, and the biologist must explain how the burden can be carried elsewhere.

options.text: The burden is carried by the same vessels, which simply work longer hours under the ban
options.misconception: assumes a ban forces hours to be worked

options.text: The burden is carried by the seabed, which absorbs the pressure as scouring
options.misconception: treats the environment as a substitute target

options.text: The burden is carried by other methods, other grounds or other fleets
The burden is carried by the market, which prices the fish more highly when fewer are caught
options.misconception: confuses a market price effect with the fishing pressure

questions.explanation: Closing one method or area usually pushes the same effort into another method, ground or fleet, so pressure can be maintained while the limit is met. Monitoring must follow the effort, not the rule.
questions.hint: Ask where the effort goes instead.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Runoff coefficient change with land cover
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a measured change in runoff coefficient after land cover change
questions.stem: Before planting, a plot produced 4 litres of runoff for 100 millimetres of rain; after planting, it produced 2 litres for the same rainfall, and the biologist must interpret the figures.

options.text: The runoff coefficient fell by half, because the runoff volume halved
options.misconception: ignores that the ratio, not the volume, is the coefficient

options.text: The runoff coefficient fell to a quarter of its old value, because the ratio of runoff to rain doubled
options.misconception: inverts the direction of the ratio change

options.text: The runoff coefficient was unchanged, because the same rainfall was applied in both cases
options.misconception: treats the applied rain as the whole definition

options.text: The runoff coefficient fell from 0.04 to 0.02, because the ratio of runoff to rainfall halved

questions.explanation: The coefficient is runoff divided by rainfall, so 4 litres against 100 millimetres gives 0.04 and 2 litres gives 0.02. The ratio halved although the applied rainfall was identical.
questions.hint: Divide runoff by the rainfall applied.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Read a diagram that links concentration, discharge and mass load
questions.stem: A diagram links discharge, concentration and load through a stream reach, and the biologist must follow the relationships.

options.text: The load depends on both the discharge and the concentration reaching that point
The load depends only on the discharge, because concentration is set by the geology upstream
options.misconception: treats concentration as fixed by geology

options.text: The load is fixed by the concentration alone, because the amount of water does not matter
options.misconception: ignores the role of discharge in the load

options.text: The load falls whenever the concentration falls, even if the discharge rises sharply
options.misconception: assumes concentration alone controls the load

questions.explanation: Mass load is the product of the flow in a unit of time and the concentration of the material, so both arrows must be followed to reach the load. A rise in one can mask a fall in the other.
questions.hint: Follow both arrows into the load.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose an incorrect compounded removal figure
questions.stem: A report claims that a three stage treatment removes 90 per cent because each stage removes 30 per cent of the original load, and the biologist must find the error.

options.text: The error is that the stages must all be measured on the same day of the week
options.misconception: invents a scheduling rule not relevant to the arithmetic

options.text: The error is that each stage acts on what the previous one passed on, not on the original load
The error is that the removal figure should be reported as a mass rather than a percentage
options.misconception: changes the reporting unit instead of the arithmetic

options.text: The error is that the final stage cannot remove anything because the load is already low
options.misconception: assumes a stage does nothing at low concentrations

questions.explanation: Each stage receives only what the previous passed on, so the survival fractions multiply: three times 0.7 leaves about 34 per cent, so 66 per cent is removed. Adding the shares overstates it.
questions.hint: Track what each stage actually receives.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the drawdown from a well's starting and current levels
questions.stem: A monitoring well started at 2.5 metres below ground and now reads 3.4 metres below ground, and the biologist must calculate the drawdown in metres.
questions.explanation: Drawdown is the increase in depth below ground since the start, so 3.4 minus 2.5 gives 0.9 metres. Comparing the current reading with a threshold figure directly would mix a level with a change.
questions.hint: Subtract the starting depth from the current depth.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a modelled baseline supplies the missing counterfactual
questions.stem: No control site exists for a long-running land management scheme, and the biologist must explain how the counterfactual can still be estimated.

answer.exemplar: A counterfactual can be reconstructed from the scheme's own pre-intervention record by fitting a model of how the measured variables would have behaved had the scheme not started, and then using that model to project the same period under scheme conditions. The strength of this approach rests on the pre-intervention period being long enough to establish the underlying relationship, and on the model not being fitted to data collected after the intervention began. The result is a modelled estimate rather than an observed one, and should be presented as such with its uncertainty.

questions.explanation: A model fitted to the pre-intervention period can project how the site would have behaved without the scheme. That projection supplies the counterfactual where no control exists.
questions.hint: The old record can stand in for a control.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Judge a landscape survey design for the adequacy of its control sites

stimulus.body: The note states that the basin was divided into four bands by elevation and that within each band two sites were chosen at random, one to be grazed and one to remain as it is. It records that the two sites in each band differ in soil type in three of the four bands, and that the random selection took place after the management areas had been drawn.

questions.stem: A basin survey design is reviewed, and the biologist must judge whether its control sites can support the comparison.

options.text: The design is adequate, because random selection inside each band guarantees matched sites
options.misconception: assumes random selection overrides the soil differences

options.text: The design is inadequate, because four elevation bands are too few to describe the basin
options.misconception: objects to the number of bands rather than the matching

options.text: The design is weakened because the sites differ in soil and were chosen after the treatment areas were fixed
The design is inadequate, because control sites cannot be located in the same basin as treated sites
options.misconception: invents a rule that controls must be elsewhere

questions.explanation: Sites differing in soil differ in what the survey measures, so the comparison is confounded, and choosing them after the areas were fixed removes that protection. Matching on soil is needed.
questions.hint: Compare the two sites on soil, not just band.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Judge which explanation fits the timing of a response
questions.stem: A population rises two years after an intervention and stays high, and the biologist must judge the timing evidence.

options.text: The timing rules out the intervention, because an effect must appear immediately
options.misconception: assumes effects appear with no delay

options.text: The timing proves the intervention, because no other change is mentioned in the report
options.misconception: treats an unmentioned cause as excluded

options.text: The timing shows nothing, because every ecological response is delayed by two years
options.misconception: invents a fixed delay for all responses

options.text: The timing is consistent with the intervention, but other causes must still be ruled out

questions.explanation: A response that appears after the intervention and persists is the expected pattern for a working intervention, so the timing fits it. Consistency is not proof, since other drivers explain it.
questions.hint: Consistent timing is not the same as proof.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Assess a compliance report for evidence of displaced activity

stimulus.body: The report records that use of the restricted activity inside the designated zone fell by half compared with the previous year. It records no information about the same activity on neighbouring land, states that the previous year was an unusually wet one, and notes that the number of recorded visits by enforcement staff also fell by half.

questions.stem: A compliance report records lower use of a restricted activity within a designated zone, and the biologist must judge whether the burden has fallen.

options.text: The fall may reflect less effort, wetter conditions or fewer checks, and no neighbouring activity is reported
The fall proves the restriction worked, because activity inside the zone is the only measure of success
options.misconception: treats one indicator as a complete evaluation

options.text: The fall is meaningless, because any change in a single year should be ignored
options.misconception: discards the data instead of interpreting it

options.text: The fall proves the restriction worked, because the zone boundary was drawn around the sensitive area
options.misconception: assumes a sensible boundary guarantees a real effect

questions.explanation: A halving of recorded activity coincides with a wetter year, fewer enforcement visits and no data on neighbouring land, so several explanations stay open. It shows less recorded activity, not less.
questions.hint: Three other things changed in that same year.

questions.topic: Runoff coefficient change with land cover
questions.learningObjective: Read a land cover to runoff diagram for the direction of change
questions.stem: A diagram links three land cover types to their infiltration and runoff behaviour, and the biologist must read the direction of change.

options.text: Forest gives the highest runoff because canopy interception sends most rain to the ground
options.misconception: treats interception as a loss rather than a delay

options.text: Forest gives the lowest runoff because interception and infiltration hold water back
Grassland and forest give the same runoff because both are vegetated covers
options.misconception: treats all vegetated cover as equivalent

options.text: Bare soil gives the lowest runoff because compacted ground slows water moving over it
options.misconception: confuses compaction with resistance to flow

questions.explanation: Forest intercepts rain on leaves and stems, holds it briefly and encourages infiltration through a deep litter layer, so little becomes runoff. Bare soil runs off quickly.
questions.hint: Follow the arrows from cover type to runoff.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose an error in a sediment assessment that omits flow
questions.stem: An assessment concludes that sediment impact has risen because the concentration has risen, and the biologist must find the error.

options.text: The error is that the concentration should have been measured in the sediment rather than the water
options.misconception: moves the measurement to the wrong medium

options.text: The error is that the assessment should have used a longer time series before reaching any conclusion
options.misconception: demands more data instead of the missing flow term

options.text: The error is that the conclusion ignores the flow, so a rising concentration need not mean more sediment
The error is that sediment impact must be judged only from the bed rather than the water column
options.misconception: invents a measurement rule that is not standard

questions.explanation: Concentration describes each unit of water while impact depends on the mass arriving, so without flow the direction of change cannot be inferred. Falling flow can hide a rising level.
questions.hint: What is missing from the assessment?

questions.explanation: Half survives the first stage, a quarter the second and an eighth the third, which is 12.5 per cent of the original load. The train as a whole therefore removes 87.5 per cent.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a monitoring scheme that can detect a breach of a drawdown threshold
questions.stem: A wetland scheme must not let the groundwater level fall more than 0.8 metres below its starting level, and the biologist must design the monitoring that can detect a breach.

answer.exemplar: Install pressure transducers in the well and in the wetland margin, logging at a short interval so that any rapid fall is captured rather than averaged away, and read the manual dipper at the same times to check the logger. Set the alarm threshold below the permitted figure so that staff are warned before the limit is reached, and keep the starting baseline, its date and its method on file so that every later drawdown is calculated against a fixed reference. Record any pumping, drought or abstraction event alongside the level data.

questions.explanation: Continuous logging at a fine interval is needed because a monthly mean or spot reading can miss a short deep drawdown. The baseline must be fixed, and an alarm below the limit gives warning.
questions.hint: Set the alarm before the limit is reached.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Judge a monitoring record for whether it contains a counterfactual

stimulus.body: The record reports the number of pollinator visits observed on the flower strip before the strip was planted, during the first summer after planting, and in the second summer after planting. It also reports the same counts from a flower strip in a neighbouring parish that was planted in the same year but is not part of the scheme.

questions.stem: A scheme claims a benefit for pollinators, and the biologist must judge whether the record contains the comparison needed.

options.text: The record contains no counterfactual, because a single site can never provide one
options.misconception: dismisses the value of single site records entirely

options.text: The record contains no counterfactual, because only two summers of data were collected
options.misconception: insists on a longer series as the only route

options.text: The record contains no counterfactual, because the counts were taken on flower strips rather than on fields
options.misconception: objects to the sampling unit rather than the comparison

options.text: The record does contain a comparison, because the neighbouring strip gives an untreated series

questions.explanation: The neighbouring strip was planted the same year and provides an untreated series, so the record does contain a counterfactual of sorts. Its weakness is that the strips sit in different parishes.
questions.hint: Is there an untreated comparison in the record?

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain what makes a control site valid
questions.stem: A biologist must choose a control site for a river restoration, and the engineer must justify the choice.

options.text: The best control is the nearest site upstream, because upstream water is unaffected by the works
options.misconception: assumes upstream means unaffected

options.text: The best control is the largest available site, because a bigger site gives a steadier mean
options.misconception: prioritises size over representativeness

options.text: The best control is a site in a different catchment, because then no influence can carry over
options.misconception: prefers an incomparable site over a matched one

options.text: The best control is a comparable site with a similar setting and an independent history

questions.explanation: A control must resemble the treated site in the factors driving the measurement, while having an independent management history. Being upstream or further away does not make a site comparable.
questions.hint: Comparable but not influenced by the works.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a response series against the intervention date
questions.stem: A colony count series shows 18, 19, 17 and 22 pairs in four years, with the intervention in year three, and the biologist must read the pattern.

options.text: The increase is clear, because the final count is well above every earlier count
options.misconception: overreads a single observation

options.text: The final increase may be real, but it needs comparison because counts vary between years anyway
The intervention failed, because the count before it was higher than the count after it
options.misconception: compares the wrong years

options.text: The intervention succeeded, because the count rose in the year after it was carried out
options.misconception: treats a single rise as proof

questions.explanation: Counts of 18, 19 and 17 show the year to year variation normal for this colony, so a rise to 22 needs a comparison or an estimate of the natural spread. The rise may be real.
questions.hint: How much do counts vary between years anyway?

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Review a prohibition report for evidence of a shifted burden

stimulus.body: The report states that the activity is now prohibited within the site boundary and that monitoring inside the boundary shows a clear fall in activity. It notes that the activity is also carried out on three neighbouring holdings that were not included in the prohibition and that no data have been collected from those holdings.

questions.stem: A prohibition on a damaging activity is issued, and the biologist must assess what the report can demonstrate.

options.text: The report demonstrates success, because the activity inside the boundary has clearly fallen
options.misconception: treats an inside-boundary fall as a total reduction

options.text: The report demonstrates nothing, because any fall inside a boundary is meaningless
options.misconception: dismisses a valid observation of reduced activity

options.text: The report shows a fall inside the boundary but cannot show the total burden has fallen
The report demonstrates failure, because the activity still occurs on neighbouring holdings
options.misconception: treats continued activity nearby as proof of failure

questions.explanation: Monitoring inside the boundary shows a real fall there, but with no data from neighbouring holdings the total effort is unknown and could be unchanged. Monitoring beyond it would complete the work.
questions.hint: What does the record not cover?
